title: Bharata refuses the throne
hook: the brother who won't take what isn't his; the sandals on the throne

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king dies, of grief, with an old curse come due. Your line was grief is the cost of love. And the one person this was all for hasn't even heard yet. Day forty-four.

Bharata has been away the whole time, at his grandfather's kingdom, far to the west. Messengers come and tell him only: come home, quickly. He rides for days with a bad feeling. He enters Ayodhya and it's silent. No music. No crowds. He goes to his mother's rooms, and Kaikeyi greets him with the news as if it were a gift. Your father is dead. Rama is in the forest. And the kingdom is yours. I did it for you. She's waiting for him to thank her. Everything she did, the wishes, the exile, a husband's death, was for this moment.
screen: `BHARATA RIDES HOME.` → `A SILENT CITY.` → `THE KINGDOM IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Bharata doesn't thank her. He's horrified. In Valmiki he turns on his mother with fury and grief: you've destroyed this family, and you've made me the reason. He performs his father's funeral rites, and then he announces what he'll do with the throne he's been handed. Nothing. It isn't mine. He gathers the mothers, the priests, the ministers and an army, and goes into the forest to bring Rama home. Lakshmana sees the army coming and assumes the worst: Bharata's come to finish us off. He hasn't. He falls at Rama's feet and begs him to come back and be king. And Rama, who loves him, says no. Our father gave his word. I have to keep it for fourteen years. They argue, two brothers each trying to give the other the kingdom. Neither will take it. So Bharata asks for one thing: Rama's sandals. He carries them back to Ayodhya on his head, places them on the throne, and rules in Rama's name, as a caretaker, not a king. He won't even live in the palace. He moves to a village outside the city, dresses like a hermit, and waits. Fourteen years. Count the voices pushing him the other way. Everyone around Bharata tells him it's his. His mother. The law. The empty throne. And he looks at it and says: not mine. The sandals on that throne are one of the most loved images in the tradition, because they are the opposite of grabbing. For many Hindus, Bharata is the Ramayana's quietest hero.
screen: `IT ISN'T MINE.` · `TWO BROTHERS, EACH GIVING IT AWAY.` · `THE SANDALS ON THE THRONE.` · `A CARETAKER, NOT A KING.` · then, large: `NOT MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refuse a thing that isn't yours. Sit and breathe. Is there something you've been handed, or tempted by, that isn't really yours? Credit for someone else's idea. A last word that belongs to someone else. A seat, a role, a bit of gossip. Picture setting it down, gently, like a pair of sandals on a chair, and walking away lighter. The bell holds the time.
Bharata refuses the throne. Handed a kingdom, he places Rama's sandals on it instead, and rules as caretaker for fourteen years.
Your line: not mine. Today, give back one thing that isn't yours, even if it's only the credit. Day forty-four.

howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Bharata as the model of selfless brotherhood; the meeting at Chitrakoot and the sandals on the throne are much-loved scenes in Ramlila and in temple art.

original.note: Sanskrit: sandals; Rama's padukas on the throne of Ayodhya.

trapdoor: what you thought: a brother who didn't want to be king.
what it means: Bharata is handed everything and says not mine, ruling as caretaker under Rama's sandals.
what a scholar hears: the padukas became a lasting image of regency on behalf of an absent rightful ruler; Valmiki places Bharata's hermit court at Nandigram.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 64–115 (Bharata's return; the funeral; Chitrakoot; the sandals; Nandigram)
